title: Amos
lead: The herdsman from Tekoa in Judah who spoke at Bethel in the reign of Jeroboam II, and the book of nine chapters that carries his name: oracles against seven nations (Judah among them) and then Israel, three sermons, five visions, and a closing promise of restoration. He is among the earliest of the prophets whose words fill a whole book.

sections.b: Amos was, in his own words, no prophet by trade and no prophet's son, but a herdsman and a tender of sycamore figs, whom the LORD took from the flock and sent to Israel (Amos 7:14-15). The book dates him by two kings and an earthquake (Amos 1:1). It moves from the roar of the LORD from Zion (1:2) through judgment on the nations and on Israel to five visions and a promise that the fallen booth of David will be raised up (9:11).
Stephen quotes Amos 5:25-27 (Acts 7:42-43) and James quotes Amos 9:11-12 at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:15-18), both in the Greek form. Martin Luther King Jr. and many others have used Amos 5:24.

Most critical scholars think the core of the book goes back to Amos, with additions made later by editors in Judah: the oracles of 1:9-12 and 2:4-5, the three hymns (4:13; 5:8-9; 9:5-6) and the epilogue of 9:11-15. Wolff and Jeremias describe stages of growth. Paul, Andersen and Freedman, and Hayes defend more of the book for Amos himself. Whether the book ends in hope in Amos's own voice is one of its chief debates.

Amos 1:2 repeats the Hebrew line of Joel 3:16, and Amos 9:13 shares words with Joel 3:18. Amos 9:12 ends with the remnant of Edom, and Obadiah, which follows, is about Edom. See the page on the Book of the Twelve.

sections.b: The Targum Jonathan, Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra read Amos closely. They take the cows of Bashan as the wives of the princes (4:1), read the earthquake of 1:1 as the one that came when Uzziah entered the Temple, and differ on whether Amos says he was no prophet or says that he had not been one (7:14). The Talmud calls the Messiah Bar Nafle, "son of the fallen", from the fallen booth of 9:11 (Sanhedrin 96b-97a).

Stephen quotes Amos 5:25-27 (Acts 7:42-43) and James quotes Amos 9:11-12 at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:15-18), both in a form close to the Greek, with changes of their own. The Hebrew of 9:12 has Israel take possession of the remnant of Edom, where the Greek has the rest of humankind seek the Lord. Martin Luther King Jr. quoted 5:24 in his speech at the March on Washington in 1963. Catholic social teaching, the social gospel, liberation theology, and Quaker and Anabaptist writers have all drawn on the book, and each use is a reading of a text first spoken to the northern kingdom.
